papers.title: Macroscopic Nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer Mediated by Coherent Magnons
papers.abstract: Phonon-mediated nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer (RET) in metal deuterides is severely constrained by inertial rest-mass dilution, lattice fracture limits, and thermal nuclear spin cancellation. Extending the generalized nuclear Dicke model to Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) magnons eliminates mass dilution via hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling while unlocking relativistic Dirac M2 coupling via Overhauser spin polarization. We derive a Suhl-clamped FMR scaling law predicting 14.2 MeV (Pd-106) and 11.4 MeV (Ni-58) breakup neutrons, 19.9 MeV alpha particles, and reconciled sub-keV fusion anomalies.

papers.title: LHC Based Antimuon-Nucleus Collider LH$\mu$C: Nucleus Options
papers.abstract: Nucleus options of the LH$\mu$C, an antimuon-hadron collider based on the LHC, are presented. Ultra-cold $\mu^+$ beams, based on the technology of the J-PARC muon $g-2$/EDM experiment as proposed for $\mu$TRISTAN, are accelerated to 1 TeV in either a $\mu$TRISTAN-type booster or a booster housed in the LH$e$C energy-recovery-linac tunnel, and collide with LHC nucleus beams in a 3 km main ring tangential to the LHC. Collisions with Pb, Xe, O and Ne beams provide centre-of-mass energies from 13.1 to 47.9 TeV, i.e. about 3.3 TeV per nucleon. Luminosities and beam-beam tune shifts are evaluated with the AloHEP software. For $\mu$-Pb collisions, the luminosity reaches $2.7\times10^{30}$ ($2.2\times10^{30}$) cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ with the $\mu$TRISTAN-type (ERL-based) booster, i.e. $5.6\times10^{32}$ ($4.5\times10^{32}$) cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ per nucleon, which a Brinkmann-Dohlus dynamic focusing scheme could increase by a factor of 2-3. The physics potential is discussed, including an extension of the kinematic reach by a factor of about 20 with respect to the LH$e$C, access to parton saturation at perturbative scales, nuclear parton distributions, photon-induced processes and charged-current flavour separation.

papers.title: Construction and Commissioning of the Warwick TPC Platform
papers.abstract: Active-target gas time projection chambers (TPCs) could provide the ultimate measurements of neutrino interactions needed for future neutrino oscillation measurements. Their development requires optimisation of the gas mixture, pressure, electric fields, and readout configuration. Warwick TPC (WarTPC) is an R\&D platform for investigating in these directions for neutrino physics and beyond. It can operate at pressures up to approximately 10 bar and features a combination of thick gas electron multipliers and a Timepix3 camera for optical readout. In this paper, we present the construction and commissioning of the WarTPC platform, describing the design and integration of its subsystems, and report the first measurements of its optical response under different operating conditions, demonstrating a stable and functioning R&D platform.

papers.title: Measurement of coincident photon-initiated processes in ultra-peripheral Pb+Pb collisions with the ATLAS detector
papers.abstract: The Lorentz-contracted electromagnetic fields of the ions in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions generate intense quasi-real photon fluxes. These lead to photon-induced interactions that are observed in ultra-peripheral collisions (UPCs), such as vector meson and lepton-pair production. The high photon flux also enables the occurrence of multiple photon-induced processes in a single collision. Presented is the first measurement of the coincident production of $\gamma\gamma \rightarrow \mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ and $\gamma+A\rightarrow\rho^{0}+A$ in UPC Pb+Pb collisions at centre-of-mass energies of 5.02 TeV and 5.36 TeV with the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The rate of the coincident process relative to the exclusive $\gamma\gamma \rightarrow \mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ process is measured differentially in intervals of forward event activity, quantified by the Zero Degree Calorimeters. The relative rate, summed over forward event activity, for the coincident $\rho^{0}$ production is measured to be $(9.3\,\pm0.4\,\mathrm{(stat.)}\,\pm0.2\,\mathrm{(syst.)})\times10^{-3}$. Correlations between the dimuon kinematic properties, such as its mass, and the coincident $\rho^{0}$ meson production rate, are also presented. These measurements confirm the presence of multi photon-induced processes in UPC collisions, and can provide new insight into the impact parameter dependence of photon-induced vector meson production.

papers.title: Complementary Approach to Anisotropic Flows in Heavy-Ion Collisions
papers.abstract: We present a complementary count of directed flow \(v_1\) and elliptic flow \(v_2\). It does not replace known methods. A fixed laboratory plane defines up--down and left--right asymmetries. A scan of the test angle is written down as a theoretical proposal. Each event is given one angle \(\alpha\) drawn uniformly on \([0,2\pi)\), the fixed plane is rotated by \(\alpha\), and the asymmetries are averaged over events. With \(\theta=\alpha\) known, the linear fit recovers \(v_n^{\mathrm{true}}\). The quadratic mean, Eq.~(5), agrees with the pair form, Eq.~(21), in which the \(1/N\) self term cancels, and both sit above \(v_n^{\mathrm{true}}\) because the event noise in \(A\) is squared. The time for one count grows linearly with the number of particles. The pair sum, and the usual two-particle correlation, grow as the square of that number. The sample is PHSD Au+Au at \(\sqrt{s_{NN}}=9.2\,\mathrm{GeV}\), \(b=4.0\)--\(5.2\,\mathrm{fm}\).

papers.title: Observation of $^{71}$Cr and expanded cross-section measurements and analysis of $^{82}$Se fragmentation
papers.abstract: Production cross sections for neutron-rich nuclei from the fragmentation of $^{82}$Se were measured, including the previously unobserved isotope $^{71}$Cr. Particle identification of the mass number ($A$), atomic number ($Z$), and ionic charge state ($q$) was performed event-by-event using measurements of energy loss, time of flight, magnetic rigidity, and total kinetic energy. These measurements, combined with previous $^{82}$Se fragmentation data, were analyzed using an abrasion-ablation formalism and the recently developed $\Delta BE$ systematics. Model dependence in both approaches was quantified through a Bayesian-inspired model averaging procedure based on eleven nuclear mass models. The $\Delta BE$ systematics provide a simple means of incorporating nuclear structure information into production-rate predictions, while the abrasion-ablation analysis provides insight into the reaction mechanisms governing the production of neutron-rich nuclei. The production cross section predictions of these two approaches are in agreement for nuclei predicted to be well-bound by the mass models. Discrepancies between the two frameworks are large for nuclei near $N=48$, corresponding to pure-$Z$ removal. The agreement of $\Delta BE_{\mathrm{sys}}$ with the experimental data and the under-prediction of the AA calculations point to a potentially incomplete description of the reaction mechanism governing the production of these isotopes. The first observation of $^{71}$Cr provides an out-of-sample test of the predictive capability of the $\Delta BE$ systematics: a cross section of $1.94\times 10^{-13}$ mb, predicted using the HFB-22 mass table and $\Delta BE_{\mathrm{sys}}$ coefficients determined before the observation of $^{71}$Cr, is consistent with the measured value reported here: $2.20^{+2.10}_{-0.75}\times10^{-13}$ mb.

papers.title: Resolving the isospin-mixing anomaly in $^{26}$Si from $^{26}$P $\beta$-decay
papers.abstract: The $\beta$-delayed one- and two-proton emission of the proton-dripline nucleus $^{26}$P provides a sensitive probe of isospin symmetry-breaking. A recent study reported the observation of a strongly isospin-mixed doublet in $^{26}$Si, comprised of the $T = 2$ Isobaric Analog State (IAS) and a state at 13380 keV, yielding a record-high isospin mixing matrix element. We report a new high-resolution measurement of the $^{26}$P $\beta$-delayed charged-particle decay performed at the Facility for Rare Isotope Beams (FRIB), shedding new light on the isospin mixing in this decay. By utilizing low-energy beam implantation from the Advanced Cryogenic Gas Stopper (ACGS), we obtained clean one-proton and two-proton decay spectra. Our high statistics study show discrepancies in decay branches and the existence of a 13380 keV state in $^{26}$Si is unsupported by our data. Our deduced branching ratio to the IAS is fully consistent with the expectation from the Fermi sum rule. Consequently, the claim of strong isospin mixing in $^{26}$Si is refuted, reinstating standard theoretical expectations for isospin mixing in nuclei.

papers.title: Few-Ion Schottky Power Scaling and Automated Reconstruction of Single-Ion Events
papers.abstract: Non-destructive Schottky diagnostics at heavy-ion storage rings is broadly exploited to measure revolution frequencies and intensities of stored ions. The mean Schottky power of incoherent stored ions is expected to be proportional to their number. An empirical examination of this response in few-ion populations is important for interpreting individual occupancy changes. We present an automated staircase reconstruction of the power in a selected frequency band of time-resolved Schottky spectra. The procedure was applied to 7008 selected injections recorded with a resonant cavity pickup at the Experimental Storage Ring at GSI during an experiment on the nuclear two-photon decay of the first excited $0^+$ state in bare $^{98}\mathrm{Mo}^{42+}$. The distribution of freely fitted level heights exhibits maxima close to integer multiples of a single-ion power scale up to approximately five ions. This is consistent with an approximately additive mean power response under the present measurement conditions. The reconstructed occupancy histories also retain population dwell intervals and resolved disappearance times for subsequent lifetime analyses.

papers.title: Why magnetic-field effects are difficult to observe in relativistic heavy-ion collisions
papers.abstract: Since a strong magnetic field is generated in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, novel phenomena have been predicted to occur in the quark-gluon plasma produced in these collisions. However, these predictions have not yet been convincingly confirmed experimentally. We reanalyze the generation and evolution of the magnetic field which plays a key role in the phenomena. Using the method of one-sided Fourier transformation, we reconcile the description in frequency and wave-vector space, which is required to properly account for the electromagnetic properties of the quark-gluon plasma, with the initial-value nature of the problem arising from the creation of the plasma medium at the moment of collision. We show that the currents induced in the quark-gluon plasma, which sustain the magnetic field, develop with a delay and are consequently less effective than usually assumed. Moreover, because the plasma initially consists predominantly of electrically neutral gluons, while charged quarks emerge at a later stage, the induced currents are further delayed. Consequently, a magnitude of the field present in the quark-gluon plasma is significantly lower than earlier estimates suggested. This may explain why magnetic-field effects are difficult to observe in relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for VAMOS++: From Data Analysis to Intelligent Instrumentation
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of nuclear-physics experiments calls for analysis methods that combine precision, efficiency, and reproducibility. This article reviews the integration of artificial intelligence into the analysis framework of the VAMOS++ large-acceptance magnetic spectrometer at GANIL and discusses its evolution toward intelligent instrumentation. Deep neural networks exploit nonlinear correlations between detector observables to reconstruct ion trajectories and identify atomic charge states and atomic numbers. These approaches achieve performance comparable to or better than conventional methods while substantially reducing manual intervention and processing time. Trajectory reconstruction reaches processing rates of millions of events per second, while particle identification using fractionally labelled events reduces analysis procedures from months or years to minutes. These advances support high-resolution isotopic identification and facilitate consistent analysis across experimental campaigns, benefiting nuclear structure, reaction dynamics, and fission studies. Ongoing developments extend this framework to detector self-calibration, using experimental data and physical constraints to determine detector responses with reduced reliance on dedicated calibration measurements or labelled reference datasets. Applications to segmented ionization chambers and tracking detectors illustrate the potential for integrating calibration, reconstruction, and performance monitoring. Together, these developments outline a path toward adaptive, self-optimizing instrumentation that can respond to changing experimental conditions and increase the scientific return of complex nuclear-physics experiments.

papers.title: Topology-based fast neutron background suppression and sterile-neutrino sensitivity in a segmented reactor ${\overline{\nu}}_{e}$ detector
papers.abstract: Reactor electron antineutrinos are commonly detected through the inverse beta decay interaction, with a prompt positron followed by delayed neutron capture. In shallow or above-ground segmented organic scintillator detectors, correlated fast neutrons are a dominant background because proton recoils can mimic the prompt IBD signal. We study topology-based machine learning using the Indian Scintillator Matrix for Reactor Anti-Neutrinos detector as a case study. A multilayer perceptron is trained on reconstructed topological observables from detailed Geant4 simulations. The $\mathrm{F_{1}}$ score and bootstrap resampling on an independent validation sample yield a fixed threshold of $P{\mathrm{IBD}}>0.40$. Applied without further optimization to an independent testing sample, the MLP retains $\mathrm{(83.4\pm 0.7)\%}$ of IBD events and rejects $\mathrm{(77.3\pm 0.7)\%}$ of fast neutron events. In a controlled spectral benchmark using an independent AmBe fast neutron spectrum, the selection reduces the net candidate-spectrum deformation by $\mathrm{84\%}$. The energy dependent signal acceptance and residual fast neutron component are subsequently incorporated into a binned likelihood, which recovers the injected IBD signal strength as $\mathrm{\hat{\alpha}=0.993^{+0.053}_{-0.048}}$, with an empirical goodness-of-fit probability of $0.434$. The expected sterile-neutrino sensitivity for the ISMRAN detector is evaluated at baselines of 13 m and 18 m, with two years of exposure at each baseline. For the nominal pre-MLP $S/B=1:2$ benchmark and the background model, retaining the classifier score in a joint ($\mathrm{E_{prompt}\times P_{IBD}}$) likelihood improves the 95\% C.L. sensitivity to $\sin^{2}2\theta_{14}$ by a logarithmically averaged 7.9\% over $0.1\leq\Delta m_{41}^{2}\leq1~\mathrm{eV}^{2}$ relative to an energy-only likelihood with the same fast neutron contamination.

papers.title: Demonstrating CBM Capabilities through $\Lambda$ Reconstruction with mCBM
authors: Yue Hang Leung (for the CBM Collaboration)
papers.abstract: The Compressed Baryonic Matter (CBM) experiment at the upcoming Facility for Antiproton and Ion Research (FAIR) is a high-rate fixed-target experiment designed to investigate nuclear matter at extreme baryon densities in relativistic nucleus-nucleus collisions. To enable high-statistics measurements of rare probes, CBM is designed to operate at event rates up to 10 MHz. This necessitates the development of fast and radiation-tolerant detectors, self-triggered front-end electronics, a free-streaming data acquisition architecture, and real-time event reconstruction capabilities. Prototype versions and pre-series productions of the CBM detector systems have been deployed in the mini-CBM demonstrator setup mCBM - an experimental precursor comprising sub-components of all major CBM systems, installed at the SIS18 facility of GSI/FAIR within the FAIR Phase-0 program. In 2024, Ni+Ni collisions at a kinetic beam energy of 1.93 AGeV and an average interaction rate of about 500 kHz were successfully recorded. This dataset enables a detailed evaluation of the operational performance of the detector systems as well as the complete CBM data chain, while the reconstruction of $\Lambda$ baryons, which constitute a relatively rare signal within the limited geometrical acceptance of mCBM, serves as a natural benchmark. This paper presents the first results on $\Lambda$ baryon reconstruction with the mCBM experiment, demonstrating the functionality of the detector technologies and the data chain for the upcoming full-scale CBM experiment.

papers.title: MR-ToF-assisted In-Source Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy at IGISOL
papers.abstract: Multi-Reflection Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometer (MR-ToF-MS) assisted in-source laser resonance ionization spectroscopy (RIS) has been implemented at the Ion Guide Isotope Separator On-Line (IGISOL) facility, University of Jyv\"askyl\"a. Exotic nuclei, produced via fusion-evaporation reactions, are stopped and neutralized in a hot-cavity catcher, and selectively laser-ionized through a multi-step resonance ionization scheme before being transported to the MR-ToF-MS device. This combination of techniques is aimed at optically probing the very exotic N=Z nuclei in the immediate vicinity of $^{100}$Sn. The laser system, hot-cavity ion source, isobaric purification and detection stages are described. A representative hyperfine-structure spectrum of the proton-rich silver isotope $^{101}$Ag is presented as a case example.

papers.title: A trap-based platform for cooling and laser spectroscopy of fast ions toward radioactive-ion applications
papers.abstract: We report on the first experiments with the Stopping and Trapping of Radioactive Isotopes for Precision Experiments (STRIPE) segmented linear Paul trap. The intent for this apparatus is to serve as an efficient capture and laser-cooling trap for radioactive isotopes produced at radioactive ion beam facilities. We demonstrate the deceleration of 10 keV ion beams and their trapping and laser cooling into Coulomb crystals. As an initial spectroscopic benchmark, the dipole-forbidden $5s$ $^2S_{1/2}$ $\rightarrow$ $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ transition in $^{88}$Sr$^+$ was driven, partially resolving the Zeeman structure and yielding a Gaussian linewidth of 14.5(8) MHz, with the residual width attributed to the ions' micromotion. The lifetime of the metastable $4d$ $^2D_{5/2}$ state was measured to be 0.325(5)$_{\mathrm{stat}}$(4)$_{\mathrm{sys}}$ s, uncorrected for collisional quenching. Several measurements to quantify the cooling timescale, the detection rate of the photon collection region and the trap storage lifetime were also performed. The developed technique will allow radioactive ion beams to be decelerated and cooled for precision spectroscopy measurements.
